stages.name: Target
stages.job: Choose the right accounts before you spend a single call. Reps miss quota twelve weeks before close, in a list that was never built properly.

tasks.text: Write the formula sentence: "We help [ICP] fix [problem] so they get [outcome]", no product names, no adjectives
Name the three problems your product removes, in the buyer's own words, not marketing language
Attach one proof point (customer, number, outcome) to each of the three problems, and know where each number came from
Translate every feature you're likely to mention into a business outcome, before the call, never live
Run the "so what" test out loud, twice in a row, without folding back into features
Rehearse the value prop out loud ~10 times so it's available under pressure
Document the ICP across six dimensions: company size, industry, tech stack, GTM motion, the specific pain, disqualifiers
Write disqualifiers in advance, so a polite maybe has a reason to come off the list
Learn the five trigger events that mean "now": funding/acquisition, hiring spike, new leadership, competitor switch or renewal, compliance deadline
Map five humans per account by name: economic buyer, champion candidate, day-to-day user, likely blocker, coach
Write one sentence of pain per persona, five different messages, not one message to five people
Set tier definitions: A = perfect fit + live trigger, B = fit without a trigger, C = neither (cut from the list)
Build your own quota-backward ladder: revenue needed → deals → opportunities → meetings → accounts → contacts, using your real conversion rates
Build the 25 A-tier account list, ten minutes per account (trigger + five humans + one opening observation)
Log every trigger with a date and all five names per account in the CRM
Give A-tier 80% of the week; B-tier gets one value touch a month and monitoring
Rebuild the list every Monday, drop converted or dead accounts, add new triggers

Review previous engagement per account before prospecting: past touchpoints, existing customer relationships, prior stalled/lost deals and why, partner relationships, check the CRM, Slack history, LinkedIn, the partner network, and your manager or predecessor

Segment the territory into three tiers: Tier 1 Value Motion (ICP fit + current signal, 15-25 accounts for an AE / 30-50 for an SDR), Tier 2 Targeted Motion (fit, no signal yet), Tier 3 Volume Motion (broad fit, templated)
Apply the time split: 70% of selling time on Tier 1, 20% on Tier 2, 10% on Tier 3
Score Tier 1 accounts 1-5 on ICP fit, buying-signal strength, deal size, and access/relationships, re-score monthly
Decide Value Motion vs. Volume Motion per account from that score, bespoke research + org map + named plan, or a templated sequence with light personalisation
Set weekly coverage targets: Tier 1 accounts touched, new Tier 2 added to sequence, Tier 3 automated touches
Work out your pipeline coverage ratio (3-4x quota) and back-solve how many accounts need to be in play
Block protected outbound/calling hours before anything else fills the calendar

blocks.title: The exercise, build it for the job you want

tasks.text: Pick a company from LinkedIn Jobs: sells to businesses, you can explain what they sell in under two minutes, the ad is live
Write the "What You Sell" sentence, the problem they remove, in your own words, not their tagline
Write the ICP Summary, size, industry, the operational condition that means they need it
Note who owns the budget vs. who feels the pain, usually different job titles
Run the prompt in Claude with your Selection Criteria tab attached, let it rate your ICP before it generates anything
Get the 25-row tiered table (10 A / 8 B / 7 C), triggers named, confidence rated
Research one A-tier account yourself, no AI: press page, careers page (8+ open roles in one function = a process breaking), the problem-owner's LinkedIn tenure, Google News last 90 days
Write what you found, or "no trigger found", into the Entry Point / Trigger column; demote to B if nothing turns up
Map five humans on that account via LinkedIn: economic buyer, champion candidate, day-to-day user, likely blocker, coach
For each: name, title, LinkedIn URL, one line on what they personally care about
Fill the blocker row even if you have to guess, it's the row people skip and the one that saves deals

blocks.title: Exercise gate · green light (Practice run, not the full Gate 1)

tasks.text: Ten accounts tiered A/B/C by your own judgement, not the AI's
At least one A-tier account with a trigger you found yourself
Five humans mapped on that account, including a named blocker

blocks.note: Reps don't miss quota in the closing stage, they miss it twelve weeks earlier, in a list they never built properly.

blocks.title: Gate 1 (Partial evidence counts as not passed)

tasks.text: 25 A-tier accounts on the list
Every A-tier account has a named, dated trigger
Five mapped humans per account, logged in the CRM
Value prop delivered out loud, from memory, without notes

blocks.note: Passed = triggers dated and in the CRM, five names per account on file, value prop said unscripted. Anything less is not a territory, it's a wish.

pitfalls: Spray and pray, volume with no fit
Big logo worship, chasing a name you can't service or reach
An opener about you, not them
One lonely contact per account instead of five
Research theatre, sixty minutes per account because research doesn't reject you, the phone does
A static list nobody has reviewed in a month

stages.name: Reach
stages.job: Earn the meeting, not the conversation. A friendly reply is the cheapest thing a buyer can give you, a date, an agenda and a second name on the invite is the actual result.

tasks.text: Map each of the five personas to the channel that actually reaches them, and write the mapping down, executives answer phones, users answer LinkedIn, technical buyers read email properly
Use the phone for urgency and tone, the only channel where a brush-off can be handled in the same breath it was given
Use email for detail and forwardability, it survives being passed on by your champion
Use LinkedIn for credibility, let them see who you are before they decide to reply
Reserve video (60 seconds, their name on screen, one insight, one ask, never a product tour) for the account you can't afford to lose
Chase the internal referral before any external channel, a forwarded note from a colleague beats your best cold sequence

Write a different message for each persona: economic buyer gets cost and risk, champion gets their day and reputation, user gets the task they hate, blocker gets what you won't break, coach gets a question and nothing else
Reach two contacts at the same time, not one then the other two weeks later
When one replies, ask them to bring the other onto the call
Ask your champion who else this affects, then ask for the introduction, not just the email address
Track champions who change companies, congratulate in week one, sell in week six
Run the 3×3 per contact: three channels, three touches, three business days
Day 1: call with the permission opener + problem statement + direct ask, then send the three-sentence email referencing the trigger
Day 3: call at a different hour, then LinkedIn message or video with one specific observation
Day 5: call the second contact at the account, then send the close-the-loop email
Run both contacts in parallel, never sequentially
No reply by the end of the sequence → move the account to B-tier monitoring, set a 60-day re-trigger, and stop nudging
Write the opener: ask permission, open on their trigger, never on your product
Write the problem statement: what people in their role tell you, what it costs, an honest "I don't know yet if that's true for you"
Ask directly for the meeting and offer two specific times, never ask if it "sounds interesting"
Write the three-sentence cold email: trigger, problem it creates, ask, no attachments or links on touch one
Write one LinkedIn message with a specific observation and no pitch; comment on their content before connecting
Prepare the four brush-off responses and rehearse asking again once, after handling, two attempts is professional, four is a problem
Write the close-the-loop email that makes a no easy to give
Never send a calendar invite without an agenda in the body; confirm the day before with something worth reading
Learn to tell within two seconds which of the four categories, brush-off, situational, product fit, existing solution, an objection falls into
Write your own Agree + Ask + Anchor line for the 3-4 objections you hear most often
Never re-pitch, argue, or lecture after an objection, agree first, always
Remember the rule of thumb: sell the next 15 minutes on a cold call, never the product
On a hang-up, log the exact date/time, their last words, and their tone in the CRM
Call back in 5-7 business days and open by referencing those specifics
Move on after a second hang-up, three calls is roughly where persistence turns into harassment

blocks.title: Prospecting tips, five moves to run this week

tasks.text: Follow the target company page and its key leaders before reaching out cold
Send a clean connection request with no pitch attached, and let it sit
Like and comment with genuine insight on their posts before your first ask
Reference one of their posts in your first real message so it lands warm, not cold
Use an event as the opener where you can, "anyone on your team want to join this webinar?" beats a cold pitch
For an account-based event, send a direct calendar invite from your own email rather than a link
Hide the guest list so it stays professional
If they accept, RSVP them through the official landing page and forward the details
If they decline, follow up immediately, "is there someone else on your team who'd be a good fit?"
Once two confirmed attendees look like a fit for each other, send a short group message introducing them ahead of the event
Use email as the fallback where LinkedIn isn't an option
Keep cold emails around 75 words, tight, focused, no fluff
Cut gimmicks and fake personalisation; get straight to the point
Where your org allows it, try a blunt, human subject line instead of a polished one
Before any discovery call, build the account's org chart, who you're meeting, who they report to, who else needs influencing
Write a tailored message per stakeholder, tied to what they specifically care about

If you're the one booking the meeting, keep researching the exec layer above your contact and hand over a rough org chart before the next person takes it further, the extra homework is what gets noticed

blocks.title: Sequence library, 8 cadences to pull from

tasks.text: Pick one sequence to start with, The Workhorse if unsure, and rebuild it end-to-end with your own product, customer stories and CTAs
Replace every placeholder with real content, then read each email out loud and rewrite anything that sounds like a robot wrote it
Put your three best customer stories, with the metric attached, in one doc to reuse across sequences
Write your CTAs in advance, a specific date beats "worth a chat?" roughly 2 to 1
Send the first 10 touches manually before automating, to catch awkward phrasing
Load 25 prospects from your target list and turn the sequence on
Track reply rate and meeting-booked rate for two weeks before you judge or iterate it

blocks.title: Stage 2 exit milestone (Measured by: connects → booked meetings, show rate, accounts with two people sequenced)

tasks.text: Invite accepted
Agenda sent
Second contact made in sequence

pitfalls: Talking about the product instead of the problem
No agenda in the invite, and no confirmation the day before
One thread, a single point of failure on the account
The same message copied across four channels, which reads as automation, not effort
Stopping the sequence on touch two, where most of them quietly die
Endless nudging after the sequence ends instead of closing the loop

stages.name: Investigate
stages.job: Find the expensive problem and put a number on it. Deals that stall in Lock almost always failed here, and were scored generously at the time.

tasks.text: Open human first, then set the meeting contract out loud: the agenda, how long, and what they get
State the three possible endings up front: it's a fit and you book a next step, it's not and they tell you straight, or you need more people and you work out who
Run the seven-layer question stack as the majority of the call, following every question with a second one
Pitch only what maps to what they just told you, enough to earn the next step, not a demo
Surface likely objections yourself before they have to (layer seven, skepticism)
Close with a dated next step and get a second name on the invite before you hang up, not after
Run a full discovery call end to end as a recorded roleplay, meeting contract through to the close
Situation, walk me through how [process] runs today; follow up on who touches it and what happens when that person is away
Struggle, where does it break down most; follow up on which one step they'd delete tomorrow, and why that one
Size, how often, and how many hours or people it takes to fix; follow up with what that's costing them
Stakes, what this looks like in 12 months if nothing changes; follow up on who upstairs feels it
Success, what specifically changes if it's solved, what metric moves, who's watching it
Structure, how a purchase like this gets approved, who else needs to be comfortable, whether budget is allocated or needs to be found
Skepticism, what they're least sure about, and what would stop this even if everyone agrees it should happen
Ask "what is that costing you" and go silent, do not rescue the buyer within three seconds
If they can't give a figure, build one together from units (frequency × hours × people × cost) and play it back for them to confirm
Map the decision process, budget position and timeline in the same call, not the next one
Look for findable events: compliance/regulatory deadlines, contract renewals, board targets, budget cycles, system end-of-life, funding milestones, headcount plans, product launches
Confirm the date, ask what happens on that date and who's accountable when it arrives
Where no event exists, build the cost of delay honestly from their own number (from the Size layer), converted to a monthly figure
Say the cost of delay out loud, then ask what would need to be true to start earlier
Never inflate the number, an honest figure they own beats a large one they'll dispute
Log the event, its date, and the cost of delay in the CRM
Problem quantified in dollars, in the buyer's own words
Compelling event dated, with a cost of delay attached
Decision process, budget position and timeline mapped

pitfalls: Collapsing questions and pitch, demoing four minutes in
No meeting contract, so the hard questions feel intrusive
Closing with "we'll catch up soon" instead of a date
Leaving with one contact when a second name could've been added in thirty seconds
Happy ears, enthusiasm mistaken for intent
Accepting the first answer, which is always the feature and never the money
Skipping the approval-process question because it feels presumptuous
Supplying the number yourself so the buyer never owns it
Claiming urgency without a date, or inventing a deadline the buyer doesn't recognise
A cost of delay built on your assumptions rather than their figures

stages.name: Prove
stages.job: Prove your solution closes their specific gap, in their words and their metrics. A verbal "they loved it" is a memory, "reply confirmed" is evidence.

tasks.text: Open with the replay, hand their problem back to them more clearly than they said it, and let them correct you
Confirm what "fixed" looks like using their own success statement and metric before showing anything
Demo only the three pains they named, nothing else goes on screen
Run every section in the same order: feature, then outcome, then their number
Stop and ask after each of the three, silence in a demo is not agreement
Close by asking which of the three matters most, then confirm the next step with a date and a second name
After each workflow, check in directly: "does this match what you described earlier?" / "is this solving the problem you mentioned with [pain]?"
Watch engagement cues throughout, body language in person, camera/audio on video, and adjust if they check out
Establish the four numbers: cost today, cost of doing nothing, cost of the fix, and how fast it pays back
Pull cost today straight from the Size layer, in their own words
Pull cost of doing nothing from Stakes plus your cost-of-delay maths
State the cost of the fix honestly, including implementation and internal effort
Express payback in months, the unit an economic buyer actually approves against
Put it on one page in four blocks: the problem and number in their language, the four numbers, why now (the compelling event date), and the first objection with the answer written together
Build the case with the champion, not for them, what people help build, they defend
Send a short written summary the same day and ask them to reply "confirmed"
Agree pilot success criteria in writing before any pilot starts, a pilot with no criteria is free consulting
Build the ROI model collaboratively with the champion, their numbers, not yours
Use conservative assumptions throughout, credibility beats optimism
Include soft benefits (speed, quality, risk reduction) only after the hard financials are established
Present the model to the economic buyer in a dedicated value conversation, never tacked onto the end of a demo
Write success criteria before the POC starts, not while it's running
Set a clear start date and end date
Name a technical owner on the prospect's side
Agree the definition of "success" with them in writing
Schedule a formal readout meeting at the end, never end a POC by email
Use the readout to convert the outcome into next commercial steps
Match proof on three dimensions: same industry, same role, same problem, two of three is usable, one is just a logo
Use the five-part story structure: who they were, what was broken, what it cost, what changed (including what was hard), the number twelve months later
Always include the hard part, honesty about the difficulty is what makes the rest credible
Keep a story bank of three stories per core pain, so you never reach for the wrong one under pressure
Treat a reference call as a trade, not a giveaway, ask for a shorter path to signature or a decision date in return
Capture new stories at the win moment in Expand, so the bank keeps refilling
Run the EB test, ask them to introduce you to the economic buyer
Run the internal-sell test, ask "how would you describe what we do to your boss?" and expect a clear answer inside 30 seconds
Run the forward test, send a one-page case or customer story and track whether they forward it internally
Run the risk test, ask "what happens if this stalls?" and listen for real personal stakes, not a shrug
Pull up your top 5 active deals and score each against all four tests
Any deal passing fewer than three tests: downgrade it in the CRM and forecast from Champion to Coach
Where you only have a Coach: coach them to articulate the internal pitch, find a different champion in the account, or be honest the deal isn't as far along as hoped
Champion confirms value in writing ("confirmed")
Economic buyer has personally seen the business case

pitfalls: Opening with the company slide, funding history and logo wall
Feature-dumping in product-menu order instead of the three named pains
Showing eleven things, which produces eleven objections
Treating silence as agreement instead of asking
A business case built for the champion instead of with them
Three of the four numbers, usually missing the cost of doing nothing, the one that creates urgency
Understating the cost of the fix, which unravels in procurement
A pilot with no agreed success criteria
Logo walls presented as proof, or stories with no number in them
Stories that skip the hard part and end up sounding like marketing
Giving away reference calls freely, which burns your best customers and buys you nothing
Assuming a Champion instead of testing for one

stages.name: Lock
stages.job: Convert stated agreement into a signed, funded, dated commitment, with every internal obstacle already handled. This is the end of the sale.

tasks.text: Start at the date they want to be live, the one you dated in the compelling event
Work backwards through the steps: business case confirmed with the EB, security/IT review started, legal & procurement engaged, commercials agreed, signature, kickoff and go live
Put an owner and a date on every step, on both sides, named people, never departments
Define the specific evidence that proves each step is done (a booked review, a named reviewer, an executed agreement), not "in progress"
Send the plan the same day you build it
Review it weekly with the champion for 15 minutes, updating owners and dates
Watch what you set as precedent from the very first conversation, not just at the negotiating table
Anchor your opening number high enough to leave room to move
Bundle any concessions together rather than conceding one at a time
Ask about their procurement, legal and finance rules before assuming what's possible
If they want a discount, trade for something back, a longer term, more seats, a faster signature, or case study rights
Cut weak, passive closing language from your vocabulary entirely
Use the assumptive close, state the next step as already happening
Use the summary close, restate confirmed value and ROI, then ask directly what's holding things back
Use the urgency close only when a real deadline exists, never an invented one
Use the option close, offer two acceptable paths instead of a plain yes/no
If a close feels hard, diagnose backwards instead of pushing harder: missing EB, weak champion, or an unresolved objection
Isolate before you concede, find out whether price is the only thing left before you move on it
Deliver the price, then stop talking, the first person to speak usually pays for it
Trade every give: discount → longer term, monthly → annual upfront or shorter ramp, pilot → written criteria + decision date, smaller scope → faster start, anything → a case study or referrals
Never move first, and never move twice without something substantial coming back
Never discount a deal with no champion and no business case, that's just a cheaper broken deal
Keep a concession log, every give and exactly what it bought; a blank line is a gift, not a trade
Send paper early, the moment commercials are directionally agreed, get the agreement into their queue
Ask the champion who owns legal and what the backlog looks like, it tells you whether your date is realistic
Know your three standard red lines and who internally can sign off on each, before their counsel is waiting
Track every redline in the mutual action plan with an owner and a date, not in an email thread
Get the two legal teams talking directly where you can, rather than relaying through you
Escalate on time, not on temperature, a redline stuck five days is a scheduling issue, raise it as one
Ask the security question in Investigate, not Lock, who reviews new vendors, and what does that process involve
Get the security contact named and the review booked in week one of the mutual action plan
Have the pack ready before it's requested: SOC 2/ISO certification, pen test summary, data residency position, DPA, sub-processor list
Introduce your own solutions engineer or security lead directly to their contact, peer to peer clears faster than seller to security
Answer questionnaires completely and quickly, a half-completed one goes to the back of the queue
Track the review as a dated step in the plan, same as any other
Debrief within a week, while the detail is still accurate rather than remembered
Capture the trigger and the path: what it was, which channel got the first reply, how many touches it took

fields.label: Which channel got the first reply

tasks.text: Capture the problem and the number in the customer's exact words, that language becomes next quarter's script
Capture what nearly killed the deal, who raised it, and what actually resolved it, the lows teach more than the highs
Brief delivery on the precise promise you made, in the customer's own words, before the handoff call
Present the debrief to the group rather than just filing it
Signed, with a start date
Funded
Security and legal cleared

pitfalls: A plan built forwards from today instead of backwards from go live
Owners listed as departments rather than named people
A plan built and never sent, or never reviewed after week one
Gifting a discount for goodwill, it buys nothing and signals there's more available
Moving on price before isolating whether price was ever the real issue
Sending legal paper late because it felt like a formality
Redlines tracked in an email thread nobody owns
Discovering the security review in week six, after the date's already public
A shared inbox instead of a named security contact
Celebrating a win without ever debriefing it
Delivery inheriting a contract instead of the promise you actually made

stages.name: Expand
stages.job: Turn one signature into retained revenue, a referable reputation and the next pipeline. The cheapest pipeline that exists, and the only pipeline your competitors can't see.

tasks.text: Run a warm handoff call with delivery and the champion in the same room, never by email
Cover block 1: why they're doing anything at all, the problem, the number, and the compelling event with its date
Cover block 2: why your company, what you were compared against and what tipped it
Cover block 3: what success looks like, the agreed criteria in the customer's language, and the metric measured at day 30
Cover block 4: the full stakeholder map, every name, role, what they wanted, and especially who nearly blocked it
Say the committed promise back out loud with both parties in the room, and let the champion correct you
Stay on the account, don't disappear the moment the contract's signed
Book day 1, day 30, day 60 and day 90 in the calendar the day the deal closes, not later
Day 1: the warm handoff call, with success criteria in writing
Day 30: first value check-in against the promised metric, ask what's slower than expected, never "how's it going"
Day 60: the win moment, capture the numbers and the quote while the result is fresh
Day 90: the expansion conversation, with the champion and one new team in the room
Go onsite for the launch where you can, and celebrate it publicly with the team
Escalate early, raise problems while they're still problems, not once they've become renewal conversations
Ask for the referral at the day-60 win moment, not at renewal, when the emotion has faded
Anchor the ask to their own number, so it's specific rather than a favour
Map the expansion across all five directions and put a name against each
Open at least one of those five directions within the month
Capture the case study while the emotion and numbers are both still high
Track champions who change companies, congratulate in week one, sell in week six
Put the expanded account back on your A-tier list in Target, the cycle restarts here
Documented win, captured while fresh
One referral asked for and answered
One expansion direction opened

pitfalls: A handoff by email, or worse, a CRM field marked closed won
Success criteria written in your language instead of theirs
The blocker left off the stakeholder map, so delivery walks in unprepared
The rep disappearing after signature, wasting everything built in Investigate and Prove
Check-ins that ask "how's it going" instead of measuring the promised metric
Assuming a quiet account is a healthy one
Treating training and education as somebody else's job
Booking the check-ins "later," which means never
Closed-won amnesia, treating the account as finished at signature
Asking for the referral at renewal, once the emotion has faded
No case study captured, so the next deal has no matched story to sell with
A champion leaves and nobody notices for six months

laws: Evidence over optimism. A good feeling is a signal, not data.
Let the milestone guide you. If it's not met, the stage is still open, however good the call felt.
Put a number on it. A problem without a number is still just a conversation.
A clear no beats an uncertain maybe. Knowing when to walk protects your time for real opportunities.
Sell the problem, not the product. People buy the removal of a cost they can name.
You're paid to advance the deal. Close every interaction with a scheduled next step.
If it's not written down, it's hard to rely on. A date and an owner in the CRM, or it's not real to anyone else.

double_rule.name: Double deep
double_rule.text: Never accept the first answer. The first is the feature; the second is the money and the emotion. Every question has a follow-up, and that's where the deal lives.

double_rule.name: Double wide
double_rule.text: Never single-thread an account. One champion is a hobby, two is a deal, three is a forecast.

deal_inspection: The trigger. What is it, and why this account over any other on the list?
The stakeholders. Who else at the account is engaged, and what did they actually say?
The number. What's the problem in dollars and their words, and what's the compelling event?
The proof. What did the champion confirm in writing, and when?
The plan. What does the mutual action plan say happens next, who owns it, by when?
The next deal. What's the referral or expansion path once this one is won?
